messages.subject: Re: QQ- Plots in Distance Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Jessie:

I take it you are trying to see all your data points in your QQ plot.  Take a
look in the Appendix of the Users Guide.  Look under "Model Definition
Properties Dialog" -> "Estimate Tab - CDS and MCDS" -> "Diagnostics - Detection
Function Tab - CDS and MCDS"

The users guide suggests
"By default, the maximum number of points to plot is 500, but that can be
changed here. Entering 0 under Maximum num points in qq plots means that all
points are plotted, regardless of how many there are."

I hope that helps.

messages.subject: Transect effort and truncation questions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance List:

I am working on an effort to estimate bird abundance and compare bird
communities among seasons in subtropical thorn forest and riparian
habitats on the Northern Jaguar Reserve in northwestern Mexico.  I
have some questions related to calculating sample effort and
truncation that I'd appreciate some feedback on.  In summer 2007, I
established 8 line transects (each ~1.5 to 2.5 km long) in
representative habitats.  Because the terrain is extremely rugged, I
placed transects along drainage channels in a non-random
fashion.  During the winter and summer seasons when bird communities
are comprised mainly of residents present throughout the season, I
sampled transects 1 time during 2-3 years.  During spring and fall,
when migrant densities vary markedly, I sampled transects up to 4
times within a season and year in an attempt to document peak
migration densities and passage times.

Effort Question:  My main goal is to calculate season-specific
estimates of density for each species along all transects combined
that are comparable among species and seasons.  Because detectability
should vary widely among seasons, I plan to use MCDS to adjust the
scale of detection functions for potential covariates such as
detection type (aural vs. visual) and season, and then stratify
estimates by season.  My question then, is how to standardize survey
effort?  For species that are present throughout the winter or summer
season, it makes sense to pool data among years for each transect and
consider survey effort as:  transect length * no. survey
events.  This I assume will estimate the average density among years
across all transects within a season.  For migrants however, this
approach could produce misleading results because populations are not
available for sampling during some time periods, even within a
season.  For example, density estimates of a migrant species that
passes through in high numbers during one survey period in spring but
is not present (or present in low numbers) during 3 other spring
sampling periods, would be ~25% of that at its peak when all effort
is pooled.  What are some options for addressing this issue?  And how
should I format these data for analyses?  One issue complicating
issue is that some species that are common migrants are in also
present in much lower numbers as winter residents.

Truncation Question:  Because my line transects are placed along
drainage bottoms that include 2-10 m wide channels that are largely
not vegetated, histograms of detection distances for many species are
"humped" shaped more like that for point transects (like Fig.2b in
Thomas et al. 2009, JApEcol).  So the shape of histograms suggest
evasive movements by birds away from observers when in fact they are
more likely the result of little vegetation being close to the
lines.  To address this problem, I can think of a few options:  1)
left truncation for species that are not found along drainage bottoms
(yet the amount of left truncation would need to vary depending on
the transect), 2) creating cutpoints or distance bins that would
group all detection close to the line in manner that would smooth the
slope of histograms, 3) no manipulation just allow adjustment terms
to fit the detection function to the data as it would similarly
shaped histograms for point transects.  Any feedback on any of these
options or other ideas would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks for your time and help!

Aaron Flesch

--

Buckland et al. 2001, Chapter 3.6.1), so it's really a simple task to
calculate it manually...

Tim

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jessie, list,

There seems to be some misconception here, as in distance sampling
analysis, effort is not recorded as time, but either as line length (for
line transects) or number of points or points*visits (for point
transects) - the exception is cue counting, but this does not seem to be=20
the case here. Hence regarding the effort question, the answer is, you=20
do not need to input time at all (unless observation time is used as a=20
covariate, but that also does not seem to be the case here).

The question regarding "strata are replicates" really depends on the=20
kind of inferences you want to perform, if you want to treat these as=20
random days from a larger possible sample of days over which inferences=20
are intended, then you are right.

Regarding the access file not opening, I have no idea what migh be going =
on.

Cheers

T.

messages.subject: Re: unequal untervals
messages.body_plain:
Hi Talia, list,

Whenever possible, estimating distances by eye should be avoided!

There is no problem in having unequal intervals. Hence your best option=20
is likely to choose cut points such that heaped values lie in the middle=20
of the corresponding intervals.

Cheers

T.

messages.subject: Re: Transect effort and truncation questions
messages.body_plain:
Dear Aaron, list,

Your effort question does not really relate to distance sampling, but to=20
sampling in general. If you have a density that changes massively over=20
time, how do you compare that whit another density that is constant over=20
time? The answer does not depend on the method used to estimate density,=20
nor with how many times you sampled each density. You need to decide=20
before hand what is the meaningful comparison. And that is something=20
which depends on your study objectives.

Regarding truncation... this is not really an issue you can solve with=20
truncation (except under very particular and non-testable assumptions!).=20
You have sampled along a feature with respect to which the animals=20
strongly respond to. This leads to complicated problems, because you no=20
longer can assume that the density of animals is uniform with respect to=20
the lines, something that in conventional distance sampling (CDS) is a=20
fair assumption given the use of a random design. In this case, CDS=20
tends to fall apart. You might want to take a look at these references:

(just a very lame promotion of my own work!)

@phdthesis{Marques2007,
   author =3D {Marques, T. A.},
   title =3D {Incorporating measurement error and density gradients in=20
distance sampling surveys},
   school =3D {University of St Andrews},
   year =3D {2007}
}

hosted here

https://research-repository.st-andrews.ac.uk/bitstream/10023/391/1/TAMARQ=
UES2007.pdf

and

@ARTICLE{Marques2010,
   author =3D {T. A. Marques and S. T. Buckland and D. L. Borchers and D.=
=20
Tosh and
	R. A. McDonald},
   title =3D {Point Transect Sampling Along Linear Features},
   journal =3D {Biometrics},
   year =3D {2010},
   volume =3D {66},
   pages =3D {1247--1255},
   doi =3D {10.1111/j.1541-0420.2009.01381.x},
}

Hope this helps

Tiago

On 24/05/2011 23:46, Aaron D. Flesch wrote:
> > Dear Distance List:
> >
> > I am working on an effort to estimate bird abundance and compare bird
> > communities among seasons in subtropical thorn forest and riparian
> > habitats on the Northern Jaguar Reserve in northwestern Mexico. I have
> > some questions related to calculating sample effort and truncation that
> > I'd appreciate some feedback on. In summer 2007, I established 8 line

> > transects (each ~1.5 to 2.5 km long) in representative habitats. Becaus=

e
> > the terrain is extremely rugged, I placed transects along drainage
> > channels in a non-random fashion. During the winter and summer seasons
> > when bird communities are comprised mainly of residents present
> > throughout the season, I sampled transects 1 time during 2-3 years.
> > During spring and fall, when migrant densities vary markedly, I sampled
> > transects up to 4 times within a season and year in an attempt to
> > document peak migration densities and passage times.
> >
> > Effort Question: My main goal is to calculate season-specific estimates
> > of density for each species along all transects combined that are
> > comparable among species and seasons. Because detectability should vary
> > widely among seasons, I plan to use MCDS to adjust the scale of
> > detection functions for potential covariates such as detection type

> > (aural vs. visual) and season, and then stratify estimates by season. M=
y
> > question then, is how to standardize survey effort? For species that ar=

e
> > present throughout the winter or summer season, it makes sense to pool
> > data among years for each transect and consider survey effort as:
> > transect length * no. survey events. This I assume will estimate the
> > average density among years across all transects within a season. For

> > migrants however, this approach could produce misleading results becaus=

e
> > populations are not available for sampling during some time periods,
> > even within a season. For example, density estimates of a migrant
> > species that passes through in high numbers during one survey period in
> > spring but is not present (or present in low numbers) during 3 other
> > spring sampling periods, would be ~25% of that at its peak when all
> > effort is pooled. What are some options for addressing this issue? And
> > how should I format these data for analyses? One issue complicating
> > issue is that some species that are common migrants are in also present
> > in much lower numbers as winter residents.
> >

> > Truncation Question: Because my line transects are placed along drainag=

e
> > bottoms that include 2-10 m wide channels that are largely not
> > vegetated, histograms of detection distances for many species are
> > "humped" shaped more like that for point transects (like Fig.2b in

> > Thomas et al. 2009, JApEcol). So the shape of histograms suggest evasiv=
e
> > movements by birds away from observers when in fact they are more likel=

y
> > the result of little vegetation being close to the lines. To address
> > this problem, I can think of a few options: 1) left truncation for
> > species that are not found along drainage bottoms (yet the amount of
> > left truncation would need to vary depending on the transect), 2)

> > creating cutpoints or distance bins that would group all detection clos=

e
> > to the line in manner that would smooth the slope of histograms, 3) no
> > manipulation just allow adjustment terms to fit the detection function
> > to the data as it would similarly shaped histograms for point transects.
> > Any feedback on any of these options or other ideas would be greatly
> > appreciated.
> >
> > Thanks for your time and help!
> >
> > Aaron Flesch
